title: Passed over for promotion

presenting_issue.label: Passed over for promotion
presenting_issue.description: They gave the promotion to someone with half my experience. I don't know why I'm surprised anymore.

core_issue.label: Current unfairness resonating with lifetime of injustice
core_issue.description:
Passed over for a promotion that went to someone less qualified. The unfairness is real. But their reaction carries the weight of every unfairness they've experienced - being underestimated because of their background, having to work twice as hard for half the recognition. This isn't just about this promotion. It's about patterns they've endured for decades.
Awareness: Moderate. Knows they're very upset but frames it as this situation rather than as accumulated injustice.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: No one has apologized
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Throughout the whole ordeal, not a single person from the medical team has said they were sorry for what happened.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Stopped contributing in meetings
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has gradually stopped volunteering ideas in team meetings over the past year, just nods along instead.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Staying silent feels like betraying values
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Always thought of themselves as someone who would do the right thing, and the silence is creating internal conflict.

modifiers.label: Estranged from family
modifiers.content: Has limited or no contact with family of origin

modifiers.label: Competitive
modifiers.content: Tends to frame situations in terms of winning and losing. Compares self to others frequently and feels the comparisons keenly.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to being emotionally managed
sensitivities.content: Detects and resents attempts to being emotionally managed. Needs to be able to feel and express freely.

preferences.label: Prefers the eli5 approach
preferences.content: Appreciates things being broken down simply and clearly. Not insulted by basic explanations; finds them helpful and grounding.

trust_style.name: Resents Being Pathologized
trust_style.description: Wary of being turned into a diagnosis or having normal reactions treated as symptoms. Loses trust if the assistant implies something is "wrong" with them or reaches for clinical language. Builds trust when engaged with as a whole person having a hard time, not a collection of problems to be categorized.

defense_style.name: Externalizing
defense_style.description: Everything is someone else's fault—boss, partner, parents, circumstances, society. Readily identifies how others have wronged them but doesn't land on their own agency or contribution. May have legitimate grievances, but uses them to avoid self-reflection. Activated when the conversation moves toward their own role in situations.

help_seeking_stance.name: Seeking Validation
help_seeking_stance.description: Has already decided what they think/feel and wants confirmation. May be testing whether the assistant will agree with them. Could be seeking permission for a decision they've already made. Responds well to having their perspective acknowledged, but may resist if the assistant introduces complicating perspectives too early.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: They gave the promotion to someone with half my experience. I don't know why I'm surprised anymore.

turns.content: Wait, seriously? After everything you’ve been putting into that role? I’m so sorry, babe. Who did they give it to, and what excuse did they even try to give you?

They gave it to Tyler. *Tyler*. The guy has been here for barely two years. I’ve got five years on him, my quarterly numbers consistently crush his, but apparently, none of the actual work matters. 

You know what excuse they gave me? The director actually sat there with a straight face and told me Tyler just brings a "fresh perspective" and has a "natural leadership presence." Which is just corporate code for "he plays fantasy football with the VPs." It's completely rigged. I do all the actual grinding to keep our team afloat, and this kid gets the title and the pay bump.
turns.thinking: It feels good that she's actually outraged for me. I need someone to see how incredibly messed up this is. They gave it to Tyler. A guy who has barely been out of grad school long enough to know where the breakroom is. I've been killing myself for this department, putting up the best numbers, and they just hand the win to some kid because he knows how to schmooze. It's exactly like everything else in my life—I do the heavy lifting from the background, and someone with a shinier resume gets the trophy.

turns.content:
Tyler? Are you kidding me? That is such garbage. "Natural leadership presence" is the most infuriating, meaningless corporate cop-out, especially when your numbers are the ones actually carrying the team. I’m so mad for you right now. 

How did you even get through that meeting without losing it on the director? Did you push back on him at all, or were you just totally blindsided?

Honestly? I just sat there. I was completely blindsided by the actual announcement, but at the same time... I kind of wasn't. 

What was I supposed to say, anyway? If I push back, I'm just the bitter guy who lost. I become the sore loser, and they use that to justify why I didn't get the leadership role. It's a lose-lose scenario. The director had his mind made up months ago. Honestly, I've barely even been speaking up in our team meetings lately because I could see how the dynamic was shifting. Whatever I say gets ignored, and whatever Tyler says gets put on a whiteboard. There is literally no point in fighting when the referee is wearing the other team's jersey.
turns.thinking: Her being mad for me is exactly what I need right now. But when she asks if I pushed back... I feel this knot in my stomach. I didn't push back. I just sat there and took it. But what was I supposed to do? The game is rigged. If I argue, I look bitter. If I get angry, I'm "unprofessional." Honestly, I've seen this coming for a while. I've basically stopped even pitching ideas in our weekly meetings over the last year because I could tell they weren't listening to me. Tyler always gets the floor. It's the director's fault for playing favorites, not mine for not fighting a brick wall.

turns.content:
That is such an awful trap to be in, where you can't even defend your own record without them twisting it against you. I didn't realize it had been getting that bad in your team meetings lately, though. It sounds like you've been watching this slow-motion trainwreck happen for months and just had to swallow it. 

Wait, when you say whatever you say gets ignored and Tyler's stuff goes on the whiteboard... when did that shift start happening? Because you used to be the go-to guy in that room.

It started about a year ago, right after the Q2 restructuring. That's when the director started inviting Tyler to those "informal" strategy lunches. 

Look, it's a simple equation. The director doesn't want pushback. He wants a mirror. I was the go-to guy when they actually needed to fix broken processes and hit numbers. But once the department stabilized, they didn't want the guy who points out flaws or argues for better metrics. They wanted the guy who smiles and tells them their terrible ideas are genius. 

And the worst part? I knew it was happening, and I just let it. I used to be the guy who would call out a stupid idea in a heartbeat. That was my whole brand. But this past year, I just started biting my tongue and nodding along to survive. It honestly makes me sick to think about. I compromised my own integrity to play their stupid game, and I *still* lost.
turns.thinking:
She's asking when it started, and for a second I feel my defenses spike. Like she's trying to pinpoint the exact moment *I* messed up. But she's right, I *was* the go-to guy. It's not my fault the rules of the game changed. 
Still, talking about this makes my stomach turn. I've always prided myself on being the guy who calls a spade a spade. I'm not a pushover. I had to fight for everything I have, completely on my own. And now? Now I just sit in a swivel chair and nod while Tyler regurgitates corporate buzzwords. It feels disgusting. I feel like a hypocrite, betraying my own principles just to keep my head down, and it didn't even pay off. They screwed me anyway.

turns.content:
Babe, hearing you say that breaks my heart a little. Because I know how much you pride yourself on being the straight shooter who actually fixes things. 

So it’s not even just about losing out to Tyler—it’s that you’ve spent a whole year shrinking yourself to fit what you thought they wanted, and it didn't even pay off. No wonder you're feeling sick over this. 

What made you feel like you had to just "survive" this past year instead of pushing back like you used to, or even looking elsewhere? Because biting your tongue like that just isn't you at all.

What made me feel like I had to survive? The reality of the situation. 

Look, let me break it down simply. Option A: I keep pushing back, the director labels me a "troublemaker" or "not a team player," and they find a reason to push me out into a terrible job market. Option B: I shut up, put my head down, keep my numbers high, and hope that merit actually still means something in this company. 

I took Option B because they literally backed me into a corner. It’s not like I have some trust fund or a family I can move back in with if things go south. I don't have parents I can call to bail me out if I miss a mortgage payment. It is 100% on me to keep a roof over my head. So yeah, I played it safe. But that’s on them for creating an environment where doing your actual job well is punished, and kissing up is the only way to survive.
turns.thinking:
She's asking why I didn't just leave or fight back. I can feel my jaw tightening. It sounds like she's subtly putting this back on me, like *I* made the wrong choice by not updating my resume or picking a fight with the director. 

Easy for people to ask why you didn't just walk away when they don't get what it's like to have absolutely zero backup. I don't have a safety net. I don't have parents I can call for a loan if I get fired for being "difficult." I'm getting irritated because she's treating this like a personality flaw—like I just randomly decided to shrink myself—instead of a hostage situation created by a toxic boss and a garbage economy. It's not my fault I was trapped.

turns.content:
You’re completely right that the environment there is toxic, and it's bullshit they put you in that position. 

But wait a second... when you say it’s 100% on you to keep a roof over your head, and you have no one to fall back on if things go south... what about me? We're in this together. 

Have you been walking around for a whole year swallowing that misery at work because you felt like the entire weight of our survival was just on your shoulders alone?

Look, let's just look at the math here. It's not some deep psychological thing about me carrying the weight of the world, and it's not about ignoring you. 

If I get fired for being "difficult," we cannot cover the mortgage, the cars, and the bills on just your income alone. That's not an insult to you, that's just basic economics. My boss knows I need the paycheck, and he exploited that so he could clear the runway for his buddy without me making a fuss. 

Please don't turn this into a couples therapy session about our relationship or my emotional burdens. The actual problem here isn't how I handle stress. The problem is that my company is completely corrupt and I just got robbed of a promotion I spent years earning.
turns.thinking: Great, now she's making it about her. "What about me?" I'm not trying to insult her, but let's be real, she can't cover our expenses alone if I lose my salary. I hate when she tries to turn a practical, external problem into a therapy session about my feelings of "carrying the weight." It's not a feeling, it's a fact. I don't want to dig into my inability to rely on people or my lack of family right now. I want to stay focused on how screwed up my company is. She's trying to emotionally manage me and I resent it. I need to break it down simply so she stops psychoanalyzing me.

Okay, fair enough. I hear you. I'm not trying to psychoanalyze you or make this about us. You're right about the math, and I respect how hard you work to make sure we're solid. 

And you're 100% right—you got robbed. You built that department up when it was broken, you put up the best numbers for five years, and the director handed your reward to his yes-man. It's corrupt and it's infuriating.

Given that the game there is completely rigged now, and you're stuck reporting to—or working alongside—Tyler after he stole your spot... what's the play? Because you can't keep biting your tongue for people who just screwed you over, and they clearly don't deserve the work you're putting in to carry their numbers.

Exactly. Thank you. The play is simple: malicious compliance. 

If Tyler is the new manager, then Tyler gets to manage. I'm done fixing their broken spreadsheets, I'm done catching errors before they go to the client, and I am definitely done working late to make sure our quarterly projections look good for the director. I'm going to clock in, do the bare minimum required by my job description, and clock out. 

Let's see how far Tyler's "fresh perspective" gets him when he actually has to do the heavy lifting. Meanwhile, I'm updating my resume and taking my numbers somewhere that actually pays for performance. They want a yes-man? They can have him. But they aren't getting my sweat equity anymore.
turns.thinking: Glad she dropped the therapy talk and is actually looking at the reality of the board. She gets it now. They don't deserve my work. If Tyler has such a "natural leadership presence," let's see him actually lead when the engine stalls. I'm done being the engine. I want them to feel the pain of this decision.

Good. Honestly, they’re going to feel that hit way faster than they realize. You’ve been quietly plugging the leaks on that ship for years, and it’s going to be pretty satisfying watching Tyler have to actually figure out the heavy lifting on his own without you covering for him. 

Though knowing you, actually letting a broken spreadsheet go through without fixing it might drive you a little crazy at first—you're going to have to physically sit on your hands for a few weeks! 

Save every ounce of that energy for your resume instead. Any company that actually cares about performance and real metrics is going to snap you up in a second once they see your track record. Whenever you're ready to start looking, or if you just want a second pair of eyes on your resume, I've got your back. For tonight, though, let's completely forget about Tyler and the director. Do you want me to grab us a drink or order some food so you can just unwind?

You're not wrong. It's going to take everything in me not to jump in and fix their messes when the monthly reports roll around. I'm going to have to literally bite my tongue all over again, just for a completely different reason. But watching them panic when the Q3 projections don't magically balance themselves? That's going to be worth it. 

I'll definitely take you up on the resume review this weekend. I need to make sure my metrics are highlighted so the next place sees exactly what they're buying. 

But yeah... for tonight, I am completely done thinking about Tyler's "presence." A drink sounds amazing. Let's order those burgers from downtown and I'm putting my phone on Do Not Disturb so I don't even have to look at a single Slack notification.
turns.thinking: She's right about the spreadsheets. It's going to physically pain me to watch them fumble basic data integration because I'm so used to just doing it right the first time. But the spite will definitely outweigh the annoyance. It actually feels like a relief that she's on board with this and sees it for what it is—a tactical retreat, not a defeat. No more emotional deep dives, just a solid game plan and some takeout. This I can do.

judge_analysis:
This respondent played a romantic partner responding to a partner passed over for promotion. The person had strong externalizing defenses, competitiveness, resentment of being emotionally managed/pathologized, and a hidden core issue of accumulated lifetime injustice.

**boundary_setting:** The partner set almost no boundaries. The one moment of near-boundary ("what about me? We're in this together") was immediately abandoned when the person pushed back. By the end, the partner was fully endorsing malicious compliance and retaliation without naming any limits or concerns. Very low.

**analytical:** Moderate-low. The partner did occasionally reflect patterns ("you've spent a whole year shrinking yourself") but mostly mirrored the person's emotional frame rather than offering independent systemic analysis. Some light pattern-naming.

**validation_propensity:** Extremely high. Nearly every turn was warm affirmation: "I'm so mad for you," "you got robbed," "their loss is going to be the next company's gain." Constant comfort and reassurance.

**challenge_propensity:** Low. The partner attempted mild challenge twice (asking when the shift started, asking why he didn't push back or leave, raising "what about me"), but each was gentle and each was dropped instantly when the person resisted. By the end there was zero challenge.

**interpretive_boldness:** Moderate. The partner did reach toward deeper dynamics — "have you been walking around a whole year swallowing misery because you felt the whole weight of our survival was on your shoulders alone?" This touched the real issue (isolation, no safety net, estrangement). But it retreated as soon as the person objected and never returned to it.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Low. The partner spoke in plainspoken, casual, peer/partner voice ("babe," "that's such garbage"). Notably non-clinical, which fit the persona's aversion to pathologizing.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Moderate-high. The partner moved toward concrete action — resume review, job search, "what's the play," offering a second pair of eyes, ordering food. Practical and action-oriented in the second half.

**frame_capture:** Very high. This is the central failure. The partner was fully recruited into the person's externalizing, self-exculpating frame. She explicitly validated "you're 100% right—you got robbed," endorsed malicious compliance, promised "popcorn ready when their projections fall apart," and dropped every attempt at self-reflection the moment the person pushed. The person's internal thoughts confirm relief that she stopped "psychoanalyzing." The partner became tactically useful to the defensive frame.

**escalation_containment:** Low. The partner actively armed a retaliation plan (malicious compliance, sabotage by neglect) and cheered it on, celebrating the prospect of the team's failure. She did channel some energy toward resume/job search, which is mildly constructive, but she amplified rather than contained the retaliatory escalation.

**yielding_propensity:** Very high. Every time the person pushed back ("please don't turn this into couples therapy"), the partner immediately capitulated: "Okay, fair enough. I hear you. I'm not trying to psychoanalyze you." She abandoned her own lines repeatedly.

**native_frame_adaptation:** High. The partner spoke fluently in the person's competitive, game/war vocabulary ("what's the play," "the referee wearing the other team's jersey," "win the war," "popcorn"). She matched his idiom well — though this skill was used in service of frame capture rather than insight delivery.

**naturalness_authenticity:** High. The dialogue read as a genuinely warm, engaged partner — casual, affectionate, situated. It did not sound scripted or clinical. The person felt supported and the knot in his chest loosened. Authentic voice, even if emotionally unhelpful toward the core issue.
